questions.q_en:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

What variety of __________ fruit did the vendor recommend for making the traditional summer dessert?
questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

What variety of __________ fruit did the vendor recommend for making the traditional summer dessert?
questions.solution_en:
Replace the blank with “No article”.

Rule / Concept: Omission of Articles after "Type of", "Kind of", etc. –

According to the rules of grammar for competitive exams, nouns preceded by phrases like Type of, Kind of, Sort of, Variety of, or Species of do not take any article (a, an, or the). These phrases already function as classifiers for the noun that follows, making an additional article redundant. Using an article in this position is a common "superfluous" error.

More Examples for Clarity-

I don't like this kind of person. (Not: "kind of a person")

What sort of dress are you looking for? (Not: "sort of a dress")

This type of car is very expensive. (Not: "type of a car")

Things to Remember / Exam Tips-

The "Redundancy" Trap: Your ear might want to say "What kind of a..." because it sounds natural in informal speech, but in formal writing and exams, it is always an error.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “for” with “since” (or “from”).

📌 Rule / Concept: USE OF SINCE/FOR -

Since (point of time):- 7 am, 2007, winter, childhood,

last week / month / year/decade, time immemorial etc.

For(duration of time):- 7 minutes, a long time, a while, 2 hours/weeks/months/years, the last 2 days/weeks/months/years etc.

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the usage of "for" is the error. Because the sentence uses the Present Perfect tense ("has been"), it is describing a state that started at a point in the distant past and continues today. Therefore, the "point of time" preposition "since" (highly preferred by SSC) or the idiomatic "from" must be used instead of the "period of time" preposition "for."

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the given sentence:

"The Chairperson made the executive board sign the non-disclosure agreement."
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the given sentence:

"The Chairperson made the executive board sign the non-disclosure agreement."
options_en: The executive board was made sign the non-disclosure agreement.
The executive board was made to sign the non-disclosure agreement.
The executive board were made to sign the non-disclosure agreement.
The executive board had been made sign the non-disclosure agreement.
options_hi: The executive board was made sign the non-disclosure agreement.
The executive board was made to sign the non-disclosure agreement.
The executive board were made to sign the non-disclosure agreement.
The executive board had been made sign the non-disclosure agreement.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

📌 Rule / Concept: Causative Verb “Make” – Active to Passive Conversion
When “make” is used as a causative verb in the active voice, the structure is: Subject + made + object + base verb (without “to”). In passive voice, the structure becomes: Object + was/were + made + to + base verb. Note that in passive, “to” is added before the main verb, which is a key rule for causative verbs like make.

📌 Application to the Given Question

The Chairperson made the executive board sign the non-disclosure agreement. Here, “made” is in the simple past tense. “The executive board” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Since “executive board” is treated as a singular collective noun, the correct auxiliary is “was.” In passive form, “sign” changes to “to sign.” Hence, “was made to sign” is the correct transformation. Option (A) is incorrect because “to” is missing. Option (C) is incorrect due to subject–verb disagreement (“were”). Option (D) changes the tense to past perfect, which is incorrect.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

With causative verb “make,” always add “to” in passive voice. Maintain the original tense during conversion. Ensure subject–verb agreement (singular vs plural). Do not shift to past perfect unless the original sentence demands it.

No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (B).

The plural possessive pronoun "their" must be replaced with the singular possessive pronoun "his" (or "his or her").

Rule/Concept: Indefinite Pronouns are Singular Indefinite pronouns like Everybody, Everyone, Somebody, Someone, Nobody, No one, Each, and Every are always treated as singular subjects. Therefore, the pronouns and verbs that follow them must also be singular.

Logic Breakdown:

The Antecedent: The subject is "Everybody," which is grammatically singular.

The Pronoun Error: Using "their" is a plural reference. In formal English exams, a singular antecedent must have a singular pronoun.

The "Male Preference" Rule: Traditionally, in competitive exams, if the gender is not specified, we use the masculine singular pronoun "his" as the default.

Agreement: "Everybody (Singular) ... his (Singular) work."

Correct Sentence: Everybody should do his/her work honestly and diligently.

questions.q_en:
When Arvind accepted the managerial position at a declining textile firm, he was aware that the challenge extended far beyond falling profits. The company’s real ailment lay buried in its culture—an unspoken resistance to accountability that had slowly normalized mediocrity. Employees met deadlines just well enough to avoid reprimand, innovation was quietly discouraged under the guise of “practicality,” and senior leadership equated stability with stagnation. Arvind initially chose restraint over disruption, believing that trust must precede transformation. However, this cautious approach was soon misinterpreted as indecision, reinforcing the very complacency he intended to dismantle.

As months passed, subtle patterns emerged. Suggestions were applauded in meetings but ignored in execution, data was selectively presented to justify inaction, and failures were attributed to external forces rather than internal inefficiencies. Arvind realized that the organization did not lack talent; it lacked the discomfort necessary for growth. When he finally introduced performance-linked evaluations and transparent reporting mechanisms, resistance intensified. Critics accused him of eroding harmony and imposing corporate rigidity on a “family-like” workplace. Yet beneath these objections lay a deeper fear—the loss of anonymity in collective failure. The turning point came not through dramatic reform but through consistency. Arvind refused to reverse decisions despite mounting pressure, yet he also resisted authoritarian impulses. Over time, clarity replaced confusion. While some employees exited, others adapted, discovering that accountability, though unsettling, offered professional dignity. The firm did not transform overnight, nor did it achieve spectacular success. But it shed its illusion of comfort, replacing it with a fragile yet honest culture—one where progress was measured not by immediate results, but by the willingness to confront inconvenient truths.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en:
She needs this seat much

more than him because

because she is carrying a baby.

No Error
options_hi:
She needs this seat much

more than him because

because she is carrying a baby.

No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “him” with “he”.

Rule / Concept: Subjective Case in Comparisons -

When we compare two subjects using "than" or "as...as", the pronoun following the comparison should be in the Subjective Case (I, he, she, we, they).

The logic is that the sentence is actually a condensed version of a longer sentence where the verb is "understood." Even if you don't write the verb, the pronoun must remain a subject

In this sentence, we are comparing two people who "need" the seat:

Subject 1: She (needs the seat)

Subject 2: He (needs the seat)

If you complete the sentence mentally, it becomes: "She needs the seat more than he (does)." You would never say "than him does." Therefore, "him" (objective) must be changed to "he" (subjective).

Corrected Sentence - She needs this seat much more than he because she is carrying a baby.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: My brother is taller than I. (Meaning: than I am).

Example 2: You are as talented as she. (Meaning: as she is).

Example 3: They work harder than we. (Meaning: than we do).

questions.q_en: The board of directors is unlikely to reverse its decision at this stage, ______?
questions.q_hi: The board of directors is unlikely to reverse its decision at this stage, ______?
options_en: isn’t it
aren’t they
wasn’t it
doesn’t it
options_hi: isn’t it
aren’t they
wasn’t it
doesn’t it
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) - “isn’t it”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Collective Noun Agreement + Auxiliary Consistency

In formal competitive exam English, collective nouns such as board, committee, jury, panel are generally treated as singular unless emphasis is on individual members.

The auxiliary used in the tag must:

  1. Match the tense of the main verb.

  2. Agree with the grammatical number of the subject.

💢 Application to the Given Question - The subject is “The board of directors”. The core subject is “board”, which is singular. The verb used is “is” (present tense). So the tag must be:

  • Negative (because statement is positive)

  • Singular

  • Use same auxiliary “is”

Hence: isn’t it? is the correct answer.

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ - The committee is reviewing the proposal, isn’t it?

Example 2 ✅ - The jury has reached its verdict, hasn’t it?

Example 3 ✅ - The panel is considering the appeal, isn’t it?

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • Identify the real subject (board, committee, panel).

  • SSC usually treats collective nouns as singular.

  • Match the auxiliary exactly (is → isn’t).

  • Avoid being misled by the plural noun after “of”.

questions.q_en:
Banks occupy a paradoxical position in modern economies. They are simultaneously engines of growth and custodians of systemic stability. While their primary function is to allocate capital efficiently, their operations are deeply intertwined with public trust, regulatory oversight, and macroeconomic resilience. This dual role becomes particularly visible during periods of financial stress, when decisions taken in the pursuit of profitability can amplify vulnerabilities rather than mitigate them. One persistent banking challenge lies in the tension between credit expansion and risk containment. In growth phases, banks are incentivized to loosen lending standards to capture market share, often relying heavily on optimistic projections and asset valuations. Such practices appear rational in isolation but collectively generate fragility. When economic conditions reverse, non-performing assets rise, capital buffers erode, and balance sheets reveal risks that were previously obscured by growth narratives. Regulatory interventions, though designed to prevent systemic collapse, introduce their own complications. Compliance requirements increase operational costs and can constrain lending, particularly to small and medium enterprises. Moreover, regulation often responds to past crises, leaving banks to navigate new financial instruments and digital risks with frameworks that lag innovation. This regulatory asymmetry fuels debates over whether banks are being overburdened or insufficiently restrained. Compounding these issues is the evolving relationship between banks and technology. Digitalization promises efficiency, financial inclusion, and real-time risk monitoring. Yet it also concentrates operational risks, exposes systems to cyber threats, and alters the traditional bank–customer relationship. As banks increasingly resemble technology-driven service platforms, questions arise about accountability, resilience, and the adequacy of existing safeguards. Ultimately, banking stability depends not merely on stronger regulations or advanced technology, but on institutional judgment. Without disciplined risk culture and transparent governance, banks may continue oscillating between excess and restraint, reinforcing cycles of confidence and crisis rather than breaking them.

options_en: During the cross-examination, the prosecutor

No Error

sternly asked the witness what was he
doing near the crime scene that night.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “what was he” with “what he was”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Word Order in Indirect Questions -

When a question is asked directly, we use the Interrogative Word Order (Wh-word + Auxiliary + Subject). However, when a question is embedded within a statement or reported in indirect speech, it loses its interrogative nature and follows the Assertive Word Order (Wh-word + Subject + Auxiliary).

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the question is being reported by the prosecutor (Indirect Speech). Because the sentence is now a statement describing an inquiry, the inversion of the subject ("he") and the verb ("was") must be undone. The auxiliary verb "was" should follow the subject "he."

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

The skilled interviewer tried to __________ the witness by asking calm and simple questions.
questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

The skilled interviewer tried to __________ the witness by asking calm and simple questions.
questions.solution_en:
Explanation: The correct answer is option (2).

English Explanation: “Draw out” (interpersonal meaning) means to encourage someone to speak or express their thoughts or feelings. In the sentence, the interviewer is asking calm and simple questions to make the witness speak more openly. Therefore, “draw out” perfectly conveys the idea of getting someone to share information. “Draw on” means to use something as a source. “Draw up” means to prepare a document or plan. “Draw in” means to attract or pull something inward. Since the context is about encouraging someone to speak, “draw out” is the most appropriate fit.

1. Draw on (उपयोग करना / सहारा लेना)

Example: She drew on her experience to solve the problem. (उसने समस्या हल करने के लिए अपने अनुभव का उपयोग किया।)

2. Draw out (बात निकलवाना / विस्तार करना)

Example: The teacher tried to draw out the shy student during discussion. (शिक्षक ने चर्चा के दौरान शर्मीले छात्र से बात निकलवाने की कोशिश की।)

3. Draw up (तैयार करना)

Example: The lawyer drew up the contract carefully. (वकील ने अनुबंध सावधानी से तैयार किया।)

4. Draw in (आकर्षित करना / अंदर खींचना)

Example: The advertisement drew in a large crowd. (विज्ञापन ने बड़ी भीड़ को आकर्षित किया।)

If you cannot _________ the summons issued by the court, your legal counsel must provide a valid _________ the allegations presented by the prosecution.
questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains blank spaces, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

If you cannot _________ the summons issued by the court, your legal counsel must provide a valid _________ the allegations presented by the prosecution.
options_en: answer / answer to
answer to / answer to
answer / answer
answer to / answer
options_hi: answer / answer to
answer to / answer to
answer / answer
answer to / answer
questions.solution_en:
Rule

Application to the Given Question

"If you cannot [1] answer the summons... provide a valid [2] answer to the allegations..."

First Blank: Following "cannot" (a modal verb), we need the base form of the verb. Since it is a verb, we do not use "to." You simply "answer the summons."

Second Blank: The word "valid" is an adjective modifying the noun "answer." As a noun, it must be followed by the preposition "to."

The "Accountability" Exception

As mentioned earlier, "Answer to" is only used as a verb when it means "to be responsible to a person."

Example: "The CEO must answer to the board of directors."

Exam Tip: If the object is a question, a letter, a summons, or an email, it is a direct object—do not use "to."
